correctness.rationale: Poisson convolution rewrites the normalized variance as sum_{i,j} P_u(theta_i-theta_j) minus 16, where u=r^2. Independently differentiating the pair potential gives weights A=P_u''(pi/2)=8u^2(1-u^2)/(1+u^2)^3 and B=P_u''(pi)=2u(1-u)/(1+u)^3. The quadratic form is A times the square-edge Laplacian plus B times the opposite-pair Laplacian: the first Fourier plane has coefficient 2A+2B, the alternating line 4A, and rotation is null. Both weights are positive and their difference gives the stated reciprocal polynomial after removing positive factors. Dividing by u^3 and writing v=u+1/u gives f(v)=v^3-4v^2-16v-16; f decreases on (2,4), is negative there, and increases from -80 to infinity on (4,infinity). This establishes the unique crossing, with u*=0.152011526727727... and r*=0.389886556228510.... Expanding the weights gives the two claimed minimum-coefficient endpoint regimes. The square variance follows from the Fourier modes divisible by four; either analytic pair energy at fixed 0<r<1 or summable Fourier derivatives justify the cubic remainder. L_1 and L_2 are Taylor coefficients, so actual Hessian eigenvalues are 2L_1 and 2L_2; read the proof's endpoint wording in that normalization. Independently computed Poisson convolutions, circulant matrices and deformation differences corroborate the formulas; the frozen checker was inspected, not executed. This is angular and local, not a global or radial optimality assertion.

value.rationale: The observable is the integrated dispersion of boundary speed on a fixed-radius Blaschke covering, and the two angular mode types describe materially different displacements of its most symmetric degree-four configuration. This result identifies the least costly direction at every radius, rules out recrossings, and identifies an isotropic configuration. The exact threshold and proof of uniqueness are useful even with general existence and known Fourier machinery; merely computing the square value or one Hessian would not supply that information.
